deep.reconstruction:
There is no mathematics on this page. It is a fair-copy prose page of history notes, probably lecture or reading notes, continuing the account of Alexander the Great's campaign against Darius III from the previous page. The handwriting is a German Kurrent hand. Nothing here identifies it as Gauss's own; it may come from another member of the household or be a stray item in the bundle, which is labelled 'Lagrange 1816'.

Content, step by step:
(1) After the battle 'at Arbela' (that is, Gaugamela, 1 October 331 BC), the Persians lost much baggage and the war chest.
(2) Alexander could either pursue Darius at once into Media, or first take the Persian capitals Ekbatana, Susa and Babylon. 'Medien' is written above a struck-through 'Macedonien'.
(3) He chose the capitals, because the Persian treasury was there.
(4) He expected resistance at Babylon, where Mazaeus had withdrawn with the cavalry ('Reuterei'). Instead Mazaeus came out to meet him and surrendered the city.
(5) Susa fell without resistance, with a treasure of 50000 talents.
(6) He then marched on Persepolis, 'capital of the empire and residence (of the kings?)'. The march was very difficult because of the high mountains (the Persian Gates).
(7) The sentence breaks off: 'Durch Verrätherei…'. It continues on the next page: 'he got it into his hands, where he seized a treasure of 100000 talents'. Some words at the lower right are struck through.

There are no derivations, formulas or computations to reconstruct.
errors: Historical, not mathematical: the battle is placed 'at Arbela'. It was actually fought at Gaugamela, roughly 100 km from Arbela (Erbil); Arbela is the traditional ancient label, so this is conventional rather than a slip.
The Persepolis treasure is given on the continuation page as 100000 talents. Ancient sources (Diodorus, Curtius) give 120000; this is a minor discrepancy.
Persepolis was the ceremonial and royal residence. Calling it the empire's 'Hauptstadt' alongside Susa is a simplification, not strictly wrong.
The 'treachery' (a captive herdsman guiding Alexander around the Persian Gates) is a standard version, so it is not an error.

results.what: Narrative history notes on Alexander's campaign after Gaugamela: surrender of Babylon by Mazaeus, capture of Susa (50000 talents), march on Persepolis
results.modern_name: Ancient history (Alexander the Great, 331–330 BC); no mathematical content
results.usually_credited_to: Arrian, Diodorus, Curtius Rufus (ancient sources); standard 19th-century school/lecture history

deep.surprise_reason: The page contains only routine historical notes on Alexander the Great, with no mathematics. It is plausibly not even in Gauss's hand. There is nothing of mathematical-historical significance.
transcription_corrections: Line 7–8: 'mit {+den+} [-seinen-] Ver-triebenen[?]' should read 'mit {+den+} [-seinen-] Reu-terei' (Reuterei = cavalry), consistent with Mazaeus commanding the Persian cavalry at Gaugamela.
Line 2: 'Kriegskasse[?]' fits the image (the war chest); the struck-through word after 'den' may be a miswriting of 'Arbela' or 'Perser'.
Line 4: the superscript correction is 'Medien' over a struck-through 'Macedonien'/'Macedonier'; the sense requires Medien (pursuit of Darius).
Line 12: the numeral is read as 50000 Talente. This is consistent with Arrian's figure for Susa, though the digits are cramped and 5000 cannot be fully excluded from the image.
Line 13: 'Residenz[?] der Könige' is uncertain; the last word may be different. The abbreviation 'Hptst.' is correct.
Last line: the struck-through words at the right (two lines) are illegible; the 'Heiligthum Lager' / 'Gebirge' readings are doubtful.
